articles.body: In a previous post, I described giving an AI agent one instruction: Implement Jira ticket ABC-123. It comes back with a tested PR, with automated review feedback already addressed. A considerable amount of preparation sits behind that sentence. The agent needs to understand how we build software in that specific organization, what business problem it is solving, and what evidence we expect when it finishes. That preparation starts before the first implementation ticket. Start with a codebase worth learning from At the beginning of a project, have the AI perform an extensive analysis of an existing codebase from another project—one that reflects the engineering standards you want to carry forward.

articles.title: What is React Query?
articles.excerpt: TanStack Query) is a popular data-fetching and server-state management library for React. It eliminates the need to write manual useEffect hooks, loading flags, or complex Redux boilerplate just to fe…
articles.body: TanStack Query) is a popular data-fetching and server-state management library for React. It eliminates the need to write manual useEffect hooks, loading flags, or complex Redux boilerplate just to fetch and cache API data. Why Use It? Unlike client state (like UI themes or form inputs), server state lives remotely, can become outdated, and is shared across components. React Query handles this automatically: • Automatic caching & deduplication. Multiple components requesting the same data share one cached network request. • Background updates. Stale data is refreshed automatically when a user refocuses the browser window or reconnects. • Built-in states. Exposes simple flags like isPending, isError, and data without manual state variables. • Optimistic updates & retries.

articles.title: Tokens per megawatt is not a benchmark: designing a split inference stack
articles.excerpt: On November 17, 2026, Cerebras published a number that should change how we talk about inference capacity. Its production deployment — AMD Instinct GPUs handling prompt prefill, Cerebras wafer-scale s…
articles.body: On November 17, 2026, Cerebras published a number that should change how we talk about inference capacity. Its production deployment — AMD Instinct GPUs handling prompt prefill, Cerebras wafer-scale systems handling decode — delivered five times the throughput per megawatt of a CS-3-only configuration, with no loss in token generation speed. The measurement came from a shared GPT-OSS-120B endpoint on November 14. I want to be careful with that number, because the interesting part is not the five. It is the per megawatt. Most inference engineering still optimizes tokens per second or tokens per dollar. Those metrics answer "how fast is my service" and "what does it cost". Neither answers "how much intelligence fits into the power envelope I actually have".

articles.title: I Gave My AI Agents an Office. Now They Ask Before Breaking Production
articles.excerpt: A few weeks ago, I left an autonomous coding agent running while I walked away to brew a cup of tea. When I came back forty minutes later, the terminal cursor was still blinking. The agent had not cra…
articles.body: A few weeks ago, I left an autonomous coding agent running while I walked away to brew a cup of tea. When I came back forty minutes later, the terminal cursor was still blinking. The agent had not crashed, and it had not finished. Instead, it had silently rewritten seventy lines of configuration, deleted three test suites because they were failing against its changes, and assumed that a database could be wiped because "in-memory SQLite is cleaner." Have you ever stared at a git diff after an AI agent ran wild and realized it would take longer to undo the damage than to write the feature by hand? I previously wrote about routing every AI agent to the cheapest model with quota . That cut my API bill, but it did not solve the operational black box.

articles.title: How moon dust and recycled cardboard could help NASA build its lunar base
articles.excerpt: The high cost of building on the moon has led to wide-ranging research on how to make use of the moon's most plentiful resource: the dusty regolith that covers its surface.
articles.body: The high cost of building on the moon has led to wide-ranging research on how to make use of the moon's most plentiful resource: the dusty regolith that covers its surface. Right now, lunar shipping runs about $544,000 per pound ($1.2 million per kilogram), so anything that astronauts can make on the moon using existing materials could help a lot. Scientists have already proposed using regolith for building 3D-printed bricks , solar arrays , and even as soil to grow potatoes . Now, a team of researchers from Purdue University in Indiana have developed an aerogel made from simulated regolith for insulating lunar habitats. New aerogels created by Purdue University researchers, made of cellulose and lunar regolith simulant, could pave the way for insulating materials made on the moon.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 28, 1967: Astronomers Jocelyn Bell and Antony Hewish disover the 1st pulsar with Little Green Men 1 signal
articles.excerpt: On November 28, 1967, astronomers found the first pulsar and they called the signal Little Green Men 1. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On November 28, 1967, astronomers found the first pulsar. A pulsar is a super-dense star that rotates super fast. As the pulsar spins, it emits two beams of light in opposite directions. When astronomers look at a pulsar, it looks like a star that's flickering on and off at a steady, constant pace. The first pulsar was observed by Jocelyn Bell Burnell and Antony Hewish. They were looking at the constellation Vulpecula when they saw a star flickering with regular pulses separated by 1.33 seconds. At first they had no idea what it was, so they jokingly nicknamed the signal Little Green Men 1. After more pulsars were discovered, they were able to rule out aliens. This chart tracked the signal of the first pulsar ever discoverered on Nov. 28, 1967.

articles.title: Space in Macy’s 100 Thanksgiving Day parades
articles.excerpt: The 100th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade is sure to be a blast, but it's a bit light on "space." Here's a look back at the nods to NASA, astronauts and spaceflight in the annual New York City event.
articles.body: The 100th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade is sure to be a blast, but it is a bit light on "space." According to previews provided by the department store chain, the founder of the New York City holiday celebration, space fans turning up or tuning in to catch sight of an astronaut or other nod to NASA will have only a returning rocket to look forward to on Saturday (Nov. 28). (The parade has been postponed two days from Thursday, Nov. 26, due to bad weather.) Not that Macy's (or the space agency) has hinted about anything cosmic planned for the 100th parade; it's only that the event has had a long history of celebrating space exploration with its floats and balloons.

articles.title: Your last chance ever to buy one of the best DSLRs? The Nikon D850 is $600 off this Black Friday
articles.excerpt: Nikon recently announced that the Nikon D850 is now discontinued — it's a powerhouse DSLR, which we dubbed an "astro master" during our testing. This might be your last chance to grab it for only $199…
articles.body: With many of the best Black Friday deals reserved for older mirrorless models, like the lowest price on the Canon EOS R6 II , a good digital single-lens reflex (DSLR) camera deal may go unnoticed. Luckily, we've spotted that our best DSLR , the Nikon D850, has a huge saving this Black Friday weekend, to help you save $600. You can get the Nikon D850 on sale right now at Amazon for $1,997. The Nikon D850 has entered its "end of life" stage, but only within the last few days, with the camera giant issuing a statement that it has been discontinued. With retailers now working through the last of their stock for this camera, this could be one of the last chances to buy it firsthand as stock runs down.
